lessons.title: Number and place value
lessons.keyIdea: The position of a digit decides its value. Each place is 10 times the place to its right.

sections.heading: Reading big numbers and decimals
sections.body: Group whole numbers in threes from the right: 3 472 615 is three million, four hundred and seventy-two thousand, six hundred and fifteen. After the decimal point the places are tenths, hundredths, thousandths.

sections.heading: Multiplying and dividing by 10, 100, 1000
sections.body: The decimal point stays still — the digits move. × 10 moves digits one place left; × 100 two places; ÷ 1000 three places right. Fill empty places with 0.

sections.heading: Rounding
sections.body: Find the digit in the place you are rounding to, then look at the next digit to the right only. 5 or more: round up. 4 or less: keep the digit the same.

sections.heading: Negative numbers
sections.body: Use a number line. Moving right is adding, moving left is subtracting. The difference between −6 and 5 is 11 because you count 6 steps to 0, then 5 more.

workedExamples.question: Round 37.462 to one decimal place.
steps: 6 is 5 or more, so round the 4 up to 5.

workedExamples.question: Calculate 0.38 × 100.
steps: × 100 moves each digit two places left.

commonMistakes: Looking at every digit when rounding instead of only the next one (6.849 → 6.8, not 6.9).
Thinking a decimal with more digits is bigger (0.609 < 0.7).
Adding zeros after the decimal point when multiplying (3.6 × 100 is 360, not 3.600).
lessons.examTip: Write 3.5 as 3.50 when comparing with 3.45 — equal numbers of decimal places make comparison easy.

lessons.title: Operations and calculation
lessons.keyIdea: Choose a sensible method, follow the order of operations, and always estimate first.

sections.heading: Order of operations
sections.body: Work out Brackets first, then × and ÷ (left to right), then + and − (left to right). 6 + 4 × 5 = 6 + 20 = 26.

sections.heading: Written multiplication
sections.body: Split the number you are multiplying by: 346 × 27 = 346 × 20 + 346 × 7. Line up the place values carefully.

sections.heading: Factors, multiples and primes
sections.body: Factors divide exactly into a number. Multiples are in its times table. A prime has exactly two factors: 1 and itself (2, 3, 5, 7, 11, 13 …). 1 is not prime.

commonMistakes: Working left to right and ignoring the order of operations.
Thinking 1 is a prime number.
Forgetting a place-value zero when multiplying by the tens digit.
lessons.examTip: In the exam, write your estimate next to the question. If your answer is far from it, check again.

lessons.title: Fractions
lessons.keyIdea: A fraction is part of a whole. To add or subtract, the denominators must be the same.

sections.heading: Equivalent fractions
sections.body: Multiply or divide the numerator and denominator by the same number: 3/4 = 6/8 = 9/12. To simplify, divide both by their highest common factor.

sections.heading: Adding and subtracting
sections.body: Find a common denominator, convert, then add or subtract the numerators only. 2/3 + 1/4 = 8/12 + 3/12 = 11/12.

sections.heading: Multiplying and dividing by a whole number
sections.body: 3/8 × 4 = 12/8 = 1 1/2 (multiply the numerator). 2/5 ÷ 2 = 1/5 (share the parts).

sections.heading: Fractions of amounts
sections.body: Divide by the denominator, multiply by the numerator. 3/5 of 40: 40 ÷ 5 = 8, 8 × 3 = 24.

workedExamples.question: Calculate 3/4 − 1/6.
steps: A common denominator of 4 and 6 is 12.

commonMistakes: Adding the denominators: 2/3 + 1/4 is not 3/7.
Forgetting to simplify when the question asks for the simplest form.
Thinking a bigger denominator means a bigger fraction.
lessons.examTip: Read whether the question wants a mixed number or the simplest form, and give exactly that.

lessons.title: Decimals and percentages
lessons.keyIdea: Fractions, decimals and percentages are three ways to write the same amount. Percent means “out of 100”.

sections.heading: Converting
sections.body: 1/2 = 0.5 = 50%. 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%. 1/5 = 0.2 = 20%. 1/10 = 0.1 = 10%. To change a decimal to a percentage, multiply by 100.

sections.heading: Calculating with decimals
sections.body: Line up the decimal points when adding or subtracting, and fill gaps with zeros (9 = 9.00). To multiply, ignore the point, multiply, then put the point back: 2.4 × 3 → 24 × 3 = 72 → 7.2.

sections.heading: Percentages of amounts
sections.body: Find 10% (÷ 10) and 1% (÷ 100), then build up. 15% = 10% + 5%. 25% = a quarter.

workedExamples.question: A $40 game is reduced by 20%. Find the sale price.

commonMistakes: Giving the discount instead of the new price.
Misaligning decimal points when adding (4.7 + 12.85).
Writing 7% as 0.7 instead of 0.07.
lessons.examTip: For “which is largest” questions, convert everything to decimals first.

lessons.title: Ratio and proportion
lessons.keyIdea: A ratio compares parts with parts. Proportion problems scale everything by the same amount.

sections.heading: Ratio
sections.body: “For every 2 red there are 3 blue” is written 2 : 3. Simplify by dividing both sides by a common factor. Order matters: red : blue is not blue : red.

sections.heading: Sharing in a ratio
sections.body: Add the parts, find one part, then multiply. Share 35 in the ratio 3 : 4 → 7 parts → 5 each → 15 and 20.

sections.heading: Direct proportion
sections.body: Find the value of one (the unit value), then multiply. 4 pens cost $6 → 1 pen $1.50 → 10 pens $15.

workedExamples.question: 3 bags of rice weigh 4.5 kg. How much do 7 bags weigh?

commonMistakes: Dividing by one side of the ratio instead of the total number of parts.
Writing the ratio the wrong way round.
Adding the same amount instead of multiplying (proportion is multiplicative).
lessons.examTip: Draw a bar model: one box per part. It makes ratio problems much clearer.

lessons.title: Sequences and expressions
lessons.keyIdea: A sequence follows a rule. Spot the difference between terms, then use it.

sections.heading: Term-to-term rule
sections.body: Describes how to get from one term to the next: 7, 11, 15 … “add 4”.

sections.heading: Position-to-term rule
sections.body: Connects the position number n to the term. For 7, 11, 15 … the rule is 4n + 3 (when n = 1, 4 + 3 = 7). This lets you find the 100th term quickly.

sections.heading: Expressions and formulae
sections.body: 4n means 4 × n. To substitute, replace the letter with the number and follow the order of operations. If n = 6, 4n − 5 = 24 − 5 = 19.

workedExamples.question: Find the rule for 5, 8, 11, 14 … and the 20th term.
steps: It goes up by 3, so start with 3n.
When n = 1, 3n = 3, but the term is 5: add 2.

commonMistakes: Using the term-to-term rule (add 3) as if it were n + 3.
Reading 4n as 46 when n = 6.
Counting the first term as position 0.
lessons.examTip: Check your position-to-term rule by testing it on the first two terms.

lessons.title: Geometry
lessons.keyIdea: Know the angle facts and the properties of shapes, and you can find any missing angle.

sections.heading: Angle facts
sections.body: Angles in a triangle add to 180°. On a straight line: 180°. Around a point: 360°. In a quadrilateral: 360°. Acute < 90°, obtuse 90°–180°, reflex > 180°.

sections.heading: Shapes
sections.body: Isosceles triangles have two equal sides and two equal angles. Squares are special rectangles. A trapezium has one pair of parallel sides; a parallelogram has two.

sections.heading: Coordinates and transformations
sections.body: (x, y): across first, then up. Translating moves a shape without turning it. Reflecting in the x-axis changes the sign of y. Rotating turns it about a point.

workedExamples.question: Two angles of a triangle are 64° and 71°. Find the third.

commonMistakes: Using 360° for a triangle.
Mixing up x and y in coordinates.
Assuming a diagram is drawn to scale when it says it is not.
lessons.examTip: Write the angle fact you used next to your working — it can earn method marks.

lessons.title: Measurement
lessons.keyIdea: Convert units before you calculate, and use the right formula for perimeter, area or volume.

sections.heading: Converting units
sections.body: 1 km = 1000 m, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 cm = 10 mm, 1 kg = 1000 g, 1 l = 1000 ml. Bigger unit → smaller unit: multiply. Smaller → bigger: divide.

sections.heading: Perimeter, area and volume
sections.body: Perimeter is the distance around (add the sides). Area of a rectangle = length × width (cm²). Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height. Volume of a cuboid = length × width × height (cm³).

sections.heading: Time
sections.body: There are 60 minutes in an hour, not 100. Count on to the next hour, then on again: 09:38 → 10:00 (22 min) → 11:15 (75 min) = 97 min.

workedExamples.question: Find the area of a triangle with base 12 cm and height 5 cm.
A film starts at 17:50 and lasts 2 h 25 min. When does it end?

commonMistakes: Mixing up area and perimeter.
Adding times as if there were 100 minutes in an hour.
Calculating with two different units (kg and g) without converting.
lessons.examTip: Always write the unit, including ² for area and ³ for volume.

lessons.title: Statistics and probability
lessons.keyIdea: Read graphs carefully, and choose the right average for the job.

sections.heading: Averages and range
sections.body: Mean: add all values, divide by how many. Median: the middle value when in order (halfway between the two middle values if there is an even number). Mode: most common. Range: largest − smallest.

sections.heading: Reading graphs
sections.body: Check the scale on the axis first — each square may stand for 2, 5 or 10. Line graphs show change over time; bar charts compare categories; pie charts show fractions of a whole.

sections.heading: Probability
sections.body: Probability = favourable outcomes ÷ total outcomes. It goes from 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). A fair dice: P(4) = 1/6.

workedExamples.question: Find the mean and median of 6, 2, 9, 4, 9.

commonMistakes: Finding the median without ordering the data.
Misreading the scale on a graph.
Giving the total instead of the mean.
lessons.examTip: For a missing value with a known mean, multiply the mean by how many values there should be.

lessons.title: Reasoning and problem-solving
lessons.keyIdea: Understand the problem, plan the steps, calculate, then check that the answer makes sense.

sections.heading: A four-step routine
sections.body: 1. Read: underline the question and the key numbers. 2. Plan: what do you need to find first? 3. Calculate: show each step. 4. Check: use an inverse or an estimate, and ask “is this sensible?”

sections.heading: Remainders in context
sections.body: If 75 eggs go in boxes of 6, 75 ÷ 6 = 12 r 3. You need 13 boxes (round up). If you have $50 and tickets cost $12, you can buy 4 (round down).

sections.heading: Explaining and spotting errors
sections.body: When asked to explain, use a calculation or example as evidence: “298 × 4 must be less than 300 × 4 = 1200.”

workedExamples.question: A school has $500. Tickets cost $12. How many can it buy, and how much is left?
I think of a number, double it and add 7 to get 31. What is it?

commonMistakes: Stopping after the first step of a multi-step problem.
Rounding the wrong way when there is a remainder.
Not checking whether the answer is sensible.
lessons.examTip: Show every step. Even if the final answer is wrong, correct working can earn marks.
